lessons.title: Using Evidence
lessons.focus: Quotations, paraphrasing, summarising and avoiding over-quoting

data.title: Using Evidence
data.summary: Students learn how to incorporate evidence into academic writing using quotations, paraphrasing, and summarising, and understand how to avoid over‑quoting.
objectives: Identify when to quote, paraphrase, or summarise source material
Insert quotations correctly with appropriate punctuation
Paraphrase a passage while keeping the original meaning
Summarise longer texts in a concise form
Balance the use of evidence to avoid over‑quoting
data.prerequisites: Students should already know how to plan an essay and write a clear thesis statement.
why: Using evidence shows that you have researched your topic and can support your arguments, which builds credibility with teachers and future readers.
Learning to quote, paraphrase, and summarise correctly also prevents plagiarism and helps you develop your own voice in academic work.
These skills are useful beyond school, such as in reports, presentations, and any situation where you need to back up claims with reliable information.

sections.heading: Why Evidence Matters
sections.body:
When you write an essay or a research paper, you are trying to convince the reader that your ideas are correct.  
Just saying *“I think this is true”* is not enough, because anyone could have an opinion.  
What makes an argument strong is **evidence** – the facts, data, or expert statements that show your claim really works.

> **Definition:** *Evidence* is any information that supports a claim. It can be numbers, results of experiments, quotations from a book, or even a real‑world example.

Why does evidence matter?  

1. **It shows you have done the work.** If you simply repeat your own thoughts, the reader cannot check whether you have looked at reliable sources. Providing evidence tells the reader, “I have researched this and I can point you to where the information comes from.”  

2. **It builds trust.** People are more likely to accept an argument when they see that it is backed by facts that can be verified. Think of a doctor who prescribes medicine: the doctor does not just say “this will help”; they show test results, clinical trials, or guidelines. The same idea works in writing.  

3. **It connects your ideas to the larger conversation.** Academic writing is a dialogue among scholars. By citing other researchers, you show how your work fits into what is already known, and you give credit to those who produced the original evidence.

> **In daily life:** Imagine you are trying to convince a friend to buy a new phone. Saying “It’s the best phone ever” is just an opinion. If you add that “the battery lasts 20 hours on a single charge, according to the manufacturer’s test, and independent reviewers gave it a 4.5‑star rating,” you have provided evidence that makes your claim believable.

There are three main ways to bring evidence into your writing:

* **Quotations** – copying the exact words of a source, enclosed in quotation marks. Use a quotation when the original wording is especially clear, powerful, or authoritative.  
* **Paraphrasing** – restating the source’s idea in your own words. This shows you understand the material and lets you fit the information smoothly into your own style.  
* **Summarising** – giving a brief overview of a larger piece of work, such as a whole article or a chapter. A summary captures the main points without the detail of a paraphrase.

Each method serves a different purpose, but all of them must be linked to a **citation** – a brief note that tells the reader where the evidence came from (author, year, page number, etc.). Citations are the bridge between your claim and the evidence; without them, the reader cannot find the original source and your argument loses credibility.

> **Remember:** Always pair a claim with at least one piece of evidence, and always give a citation. A claim without evidence is just an opinion; evidence without a citation is plagiarism.

In short, evidence is the backbone of academic writing. It proves your points, earns the reader’s trust, and places your work within the ongoing scholarly conversation. By mastering quotations, paraphrasing, and summarising, you will be able to use evidence effectively and responsibly.

sections.heading: Quotations
sections.body:
When you want to support an idea in your essay, a **quotation** is a short piece of someone else’s exact words that you copy into your own writing.  

> **Definition:** A quotation is a verbatim (exact) excerpt from a source, placed inside quotation marks and followed by a citation that tells the reader where it came from.  

Why use a quotation?  
- It shows that you have read reliable sources.  
- It lets the reader hear the original voice, which can be more persuasive than your own summary.  
- It can provide a precise term or phrase that would be clumsy to re‑phrase.

### Choose a short, relevant quote  

1. **Read the source carefully.** Look for a sentence or phrase that directly backs the point you are making.  
2. **Check the length.** A good quotation is usually no longer than one or two sentences (about 20‑30 words). Longer passages should be shortened or paraphrased.  
3. **Make sure it is relevant.** The quote must relate clearly to the claim you are supporting; otherwise it will confuse the reader.

> **In daily life:** Think of a quotation like a tiny piece of a puzzle that fits exactly into the picture you are building. If the piece is too big or from a different puzzle, the picture looks wrong.

### Embed the quote in your own sentence  

A quotation should never stand alone as a separate paragraph unless you are using a block quote (which is for longer excerpts and is not needed for short quotes). Instead, weave it into the flow of your own sentence.

**Step‑by‑step example**

Suppose you are writing about the importance of sleep for students. You have found this sentence in a research article:

> “Students who get at least eight hours of sleep perform better on exams than those who sleep less” (Smith 2022, 45).

**Embedding it**

1. **Introduce the quote** with your own words.  
   - *Research shows that…*  
2. **Insert the quotation** inside quotation marks.  
   - *Research shows that “students who get at least eight hours of sleep perform better on exams than those who sleep less” (Smith 2022, 45).*  

Now the quote is part of a larger sentence that explains why you are mentioning it.

### Use quotation marks and citations correctly  

- **Quotation marks**: Double quotes “ ” go around the exact words you are copying.  
- **Citation**: Immediately after the closing quote, place a parenthetical citation (author’s last name, year, page number) or a footnote, depending on the style guide you follow (APA, MLA, Chicago, etc.).  

> **Note:** If the quote is longer than 40 words in MLA or 30 words in APA, you must format it as a block quote, which is indented and does not use quotation marks. For this lesson we focus on short quotes that stay inside the paragraph.

### Punctuate around the quote  

- If the quotation ends a sentence, place the period **after** the citation, not inside the quotation marks.  
  - Correct: *… “sleep is essential for learning” (Jones 2019, 12).*  
  - Incorrect: *… “sleep is essential for learning.” (Jones 2019, 12).*  

- If the quotation is only part of a sentence, keep the punctuation inside the quote as it appears in the source.  

### Practice embedding  

| Your claim | Quote to embed | Integrated sentence |
|------------|----------------|---------------------|
| Climate change is accelerating. | “The rate of global warming has doubled in the past decade” (Lee 2021, 78) | Climate scientists warn that “the rate of global warming has doubled in the past decade” (Lee 2021, 78). |
| Social media can affect self‑esteem. | “Teens who spend more than three hours daily on Instagram report lower confidence” (Brown 2020, 102) | Studies reveal that “teens who spend more than three hours daily on Instagram report lower confidence” (Brown 2020, 102). |

### Common pitfalls  

> **Common mistake:** Using a long passage without trimming it, or dropping the quotation marks.  
If you copy a whole paragraph, you are likely over‑quoting and may need to paraphrase instead. Always keep the marks; otherwise the reader cannot tell which words are yours and which are borrowed.

### Quick checklist before you finish  

- [ ] Is the quote **short** (≤ 2 sentences)?  
- [ ] Does it **directly support** the point you just made?  
- [ ] Are the **quotation marks** placed correctly?  
- [ ] Is the **citation** complete and in the right style?  
- [ ] Have you **punctuated** the sentence according to the rules above?  

> **Remember:** A well‑chosen quotation is like a tiny, shining gem that adds sparkle to your argument—use it sparingly, place it carefully, and always give credit.

sections.heading: Paraphrasing
sections.body:
Paraphrasing means taking someone else’s idea and writing it again **in your own words** while keeping the original meaning.  
It is different from copying a sentence word‑for‑word (that would be a quotation) and also different from just shortening the idea (that would be a summary).  

> **Definition:** *Paraphrase* – a restatement of a source’s idea using new wording and sentence structure, followed by a citation that shows where the idea came from.  

Why paraphrase?  
When you paraphrase, you show that you understand the material well enough to explain it yourself. This helps readers see how the source fits into your own argument, and it avoids over‑loading your paper with long quotations that can drown out your voice.  

**Step‑by‑step process**

1. **Read the original passage carefully.**  
   Read it at least twice. Ask yourself: *What is the main point the author is making?*  

2. **Put the passage away.**  
   Try to write the idea down without looking at the text. This forces you to use your own phrasing.  

3. **Check your version against the original.**  
   Make sure you have kept the same meaning and have not added new ideas or omitted important details.  

4. **Add a citation.**  
   Even though the words are yours, the idea is not. Use the citation style required by your teacher (APA, MLA, Chicago, etc.). For example, in APA you would write:  

   $$\text{(Author, Year)}$$  

   In MLA you would write:  

   $$\text{(Author Page)}$$  

5. **Compare sentence structure.**  
   If the original sentence used a passive voice (“The experiment was conducted by the researchers”), you might switch to active voice (“The researchers conducted the experiment”). Changing voice, order of clauses, or using synonyms are all ways to make the wording fresh.  

> **Note:** A good paraphrase does **not** just replace a few words with synonyms. It rewrites the whole sentence or paragraph while preserving the original intent.  

**Everyday comparison**  
Think of paraphrasing like retelling a story you heard from a friend. If your friend says, “I saw a huge, orange cat sitting on the roof,” you might tell someone else, “My friend spotted a big orange cat on the roof.” You changed the words, but the core information stays the same.  

**Common mistake**  
A frequent error is *patchwriting*: copying most of the original sentence and only swapping a few words. This still counts as plagiarism because the structure and many words are unchanged.  

> **Common mistake:** *Patchwriting* – replacing only a handful of words while keeping the original sentence structure; this is still considered copying.  

**How to avoid it**  
- After writing your paraphrase, highlight any words that also appear in the source. If more than a few short words match, try to re‑express the idea again.  
- Use a different sentence length. If the original is long, you might break it into two shorter sentences, or combine two short sentences into one.  

**Citing the paraphrase**  
Even though you have rewritten the text, you must still give credit. The citation tells the reader where the idea originated. In most styles, the citation appears at the end of the paraphrased passage, inside parentheses.  

> **Remember:** Every paraphrase needs a citation, because the ideas belong to the original author.  

**Practice exercise**  
Original: “Climate change is accelerating the melting of polar ice caps, which raises sea levels and threatens coastal communities worldwide.”  

Your paraphrase: *Write the idea in your own words, then add a citation.*  

Check that you have:  
- Changed the wording and sentence structure.  
- Kept the meaning (melting ice, rising sea levels, threat to coasts).  
- Included a citation like (Smith 2022).  

By following these small, clear steps, paraphrasing becomes a reliable tool for building strong, evidence‑based essays while respecting the work of other scholars.

sections.heading: Summarising
sections.body:
Summarising means taking a longer piece of text—such as a paragraph, a chapter, or even an entire article—and turning it into a short paragraph that tells the reader only the most important ideas.  

First, read the original passage carefully. Ask yourself: *What is the main argument?* *What evidence does the author use to support it?* *What conclusions are drawn?* Anything that repeats the same point, gives extra detail, or tells a story that does not affect the main argument can be left out.  

Next, write the summary in your own words. This is different from copying a sentence verbatim; you must change the wording while keeping the original meaning. Using your own words shows that you have understood the material, and it also avoids plagiarism.  

When you finish the short paragraph, you must still give credit to the source. A typical in‑text citation for a summary looks like this:  

$$ (Author, Year) $$  

For example, if you summarise a study by Lee published in 2020, you would end the paragraph with *(Lee, 2020)*. This tells the reader where the ideas came from, even though you have not quoted any exact words.  

> **Definition:** Summarising is condensing a longer text into a brief overview that captures only the main points, while still citing the original source.  

Why is summarising useful? In an essay you often need to show that you have read several sources, but you cannot include every detail from each one. Summaries let you bring many ideas together in a manageable length, helping the reader see the big picture.  

Think of summarising like making a movie trailer. A trailer shows the most exciting scenes and tells you what the film is about, but it does not include every dialogue line or every subplot. The goal is to give the audience enough information to decide whether they want to watch the full movie. In the same way, a summary gives your reader enough of the original argument to understand it, without overwhelming them with every example or statistic.  

Here is a step‑by‑step method you can follow:  

1. **Read** the passage once for general meaning.  
2. **Highlight** or underline sentences that state the main claim, key evidence, and conclusion.  
3. **Write** a one‑sentence statement of the main claim in your own words.  
4. **Add** one or two sentences that describe the most important evidence or reasoning.  
5. **Conclude** with the author’s final point or implication, again in your own words.  
6. **Cite** the source using the appropriate format (e.g., *(Author, Year)*).  

> **In daily life:** When you tell a friend what a news article was about, you naturally summarise it— you give the headline, the main fact, and why it matters, without reading every paragraph aloud.  

A common mistake is to include too many details, turning the summary back into a paraphrase or a mini‑copy of the original. This defeats the purpose of a summary and can make your essay feel bloated.  

> **Common mistake:** Adding unnecessary examples or minor data points that do not affect the main argument.  

Another pitfall is forgetting to cite the source. Even though you have not used the exact words, the ideas are still someone else’s, so you must give credit.  

> **Remember:** Always end a summary with a citation, even if you have changed every word.  

Finally, check your work. Does the summary convey the same overall meaning as the original? Is it significantly shorter—usually about one‑third to one‑quarter of the original length? If you can answer “yes” to both questions, you have written a good summary.  

Using summaries effectively lets you build a strong, evidence‑based argument while keeping your writing clear and concise. Practice with short articles first, then move on to longer chapters, and you will soon be able to condense complex material into neat, readable overviews.

sections.heading: Balancing Evidence and Avoiding Over‑Quoting
sections.body:
When you write an academic paragraph, the **main job** of the paragraph is to show *your own thinking*. Evidence – quotes, paraphrases, and summaries – are tools that help you prove the point you are making, not the point itself. Think of evidence like the ingredients in a recipe: the chef (you) decides what dish to serve, and the ingredients just give flavor and texture. If you put too many ingredients and forget the main flavor you wanted, the dish becomes confusing. The same happens in writing: if you let the quoted words speak for themselves, the reader may wonder what *you* think about them.

> **Remember:** Your analysis must be the biggest part of the paragraph; evidence should support, not replace, it.

### 1. Start with a clear claim  
Begin the paragraph with a single sentence that tells the reader *what you are arguing*. This is called the **topic sentence**. It sets the direction for everything that follows. For example:  

*“The author’s use of irony reveals the hidden fear of failure in the protagonist.”*  

Now the reader knows the point you will explain.

### 2. Choose the right kind of evidence  
- **Quotation** – copy the exact words, enclosed in quotation marks, and give a citation. Use it when the original wording is especially powerful, precise, or when you need to discuss the language itself.  
- **Paraphrase** – rewrite the idea in your own words, still giving a citation. Use it when the content is important but the exact wording is not crucial.  
- **Summary** – condense a larger passage or whole chapter into a brief overview, also cited. Use it when you need background or to show the overall argument of a source.

### 3. Mix them in a balanced way  
A good paragraph often follows a simple pattern:

1. **Claim** (your own words)  
2. **Evidence** (quote, paraphrase, or summary)  
3. **Explanation** (your analysis)  
4. **Another piece of evidence** (different type)  
5. **Further explanation**  

By alternating evidence and explanation, you keep the focus on your ideas. For instance:

> “The narrator describes the city as ‘a maze of broken streets’ (Smith 45), suggesting confusion. This image mirrors the protagonist’s inner turmoil, because a maze has many dead‑ends, just as the character feels trapped by his choices.”

Here the quote is followed immediately by an explanation that links the quote to the claim.

### 4. Keep the quote short  
Long quotations can drown your voice. If a passage is longer than three lines, consider **summarising** it instead, then pick a short phrase to quote if a specific word choice matters.  

> **Common mistake:** Using a block quote (more than three lines) for a point that could be expressed in a sentence or two. This makes the paragraph look like a collage of other people’s words.

### 5. Check the “evidence‑to‑analysis ratio”  
After you finish the paragraph, read it aloud and ask:

- Does the paragraph start and end with *my* ideas?  
- For every piece of evidence, is there a sentence that explains **why** it matters?  

If you find a quote that is not followed by an explanation, add a sentence that connects it back to your claim. If you have more evidence than analysis, combine some pieces of evidence and write a longer explanation.

### 6. Use a “voice‑check” worksheet  
Create a simple table while drafting:

| Evidence type | What it says (in brief) | How it supports my claim |
|---------------|------------------------|--------------------------|
| Quote         | “...”                  | Shows …                  |
| Paraphrase    | …                      | Shows …                  |
| Summary       | …                      | Shows …                  |

If any row has a blank in the “How it supports” column, you have an **orphaned** piece of evidence that needs analysis.

### 7. End with a concluding sentence  
Wrap up the paragraph by restating the main point in a new way, showing how the evidence and your analysis together prove it. This reinforces that **your voice** is the thread that holds everything together.

> **In daily life:** Think of a conversation where you share a news article. You might quote a striking line, then tell your friend why it matters to the story you’re discussing. You wouldn’t just read the article aloud without adding your own comment. The same principle works in academic writing.

practice.q: Why is it important to use evidence when you make a claim in an essay?
practice.a: Using evidence shows that your claim is not just an opinion but is supported by facts or expert opinions. First, you state your claim. Second, you add evidence (a quotation, statistic, or study) that backs it up. Third, you explain how the evidence connects to the claim. This makes your argument more convincing and helps the reader trust your writing.

practice.q: What is the difference between paraphrasing and summarising?
practice.a: Paraphrasing means rewriting a specific passage in your own words while keeping the original length and detail. Summarising means condensing the main ideas of a longer text into a brief overview, leaving out most details. Both require a citation, but paraphrasing retains the full meaning of a single idea, whereas summarising captures the overall gist.

practice.q: You have the sentence: “Climate change is accelerating, with global temperatures rising 1.2°C above pre‑industrial levels.” Show how to incorporate this as a quotation and as a paraphrase in a paragraph, including proper citation.
practice.a: Quotation: According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (2023), “climate change is accelerating, with global temperatures rising 1.2°C above pre‑industrial levels” (p. 45). Paraphrase: The IPCC (2023) reports that the planet’s temperature has increased by about 1.2°C compared with the pre‑industrial era, indicating a rapid acceleration of climate change. In both cases you give credit to the source and place the information in your own sentence.

practice.q: Explain how over‑quoting can weaken an essay, and give one strategy to avoid it.
practice.a: Over‑quoting means using too many long quotations, which can drown out your own voice and make the essay feel like a collection of other people’s words. It also reduces the space for your analysis. One strategy to avoid over‑quoting is to use quotations only when the original wording is especially powerful or precise, and to paraphrase or summarise the rest, always adding your own explanation of why the evidence matters.

practice.q: In a 500‑word essay on the benefits of renewable energy, you have three sources: a government report with statistics, a scientist’s interview, and a news article with a personal story. Plan how you would balance quotations, paraphrases, and summaries from these sources, and justify your choices.
practice.a: First, use the government report for a summary: “Recent data show that renewable energy now supplies 30% of the nation’s electricity” (Dept. of Energy, 2022). This gives a concise factual backdrop. Second, select a short, impactful quotation from the scientist’s interview: “Solar power is the most scalable clean energy solution we have today” (Dr. Lee, 2023). This adds authority and a memorable phrase. Third, paraphrase the news article’s personal story, keeping the main point: a family reduced their bills by 40% after installing solar panels (Smith, 2023). This illustrates real‑world impact without using a long quote. By summarising the report, quoting the expert, and paraphrasing the anecdote, you provide a mix of data, authority, and human interest while keeping your own analysis dominant.

practice.q: A peer reviewer says your essay relies too heavily on paraphrasing and not enough on direct quotations. How would you evaluate this feedback and decide whether to add more quotations? Provide a step‑by‑step approach.
practice.a: Step 1: Review the assignment guidelines to see if a specific ratio of quotes to paraphrase is required. Step 2: Identify the parts of your essay where the original wording is especially powerful, precise, or memorable; these are good spots for quotations. Step 3: Check whether any key definitions or unique phrasing from sources have been paraphrased; consider restoring them as quotes with citations. Step 4: Ensure that any added quotations are brief and directly support your argument; avoid long blocks of text. Step 5: Revise the essay by inserting the selected quotations, then re‑read to confirm your own voice still leads the discussion. This systematic check lets you balance the reviewer’s concern with the need to keep your analysis central.

data.recap: This lesson explains why evidence is essential in academic writing and defines evidence, quotations, paraphrasing, and summarising. It shows how to choose short, relevant quotes, how to paraphrase correctly, and how to create concise summaries. The section on balancing evidence stresses that your own analysis should dominate, with evidence used only to support your points. Finally, it outlines steps for building a strong paragraph with a clear claim and appropriate evidence.

lessons.title: Citing Sources
lessons.focus: Referencing styles, in-text citations and building a reference list

data.title: Citing Sources
data.summary: In this lesson students learn about different referencing styles, how to place in‑text citations correctly, and how to compile a complete reference list. They will practice applying these skills to avoid plagiarism and give credit to sources.
objectives: Identify the main features of common referencing styles such as APA, MLA and Harvard
Create correct in‑text citations for quotes, paraphrases and summaries
Assemble a properly formatted reference list for a range of source types
Compare the differences between citation styles and choose the appropriate one for a given task
data.prerequisites: Students should already know how to use evidence in an essay and understand why giving credit to authors is important.
why: Accurate citation shows respect for other people's ideas and helps readers verify information, which is essential in academic and professional work.
Employers and universities expect proper referencing; mastering it now prevents plagiarism issues and builds credibility for future research or reports.

sections.heading: What is a Referencing Style?
sections.body:
When you write a school essay, a lab report, or a short research paper, you do not just list your own ideas. You also need to show where the facts, theories, or quotations you use come from. A **referencing style** is the set of rules that tells you exactly how to do that.  

> **Definition:** A referencing style is a collection of guidelines for citing (showing) sources inside the text and for arranging those sources in a reference list at the end of your work.  

These rules cover things such as:  

* the order of the author’s name, the year, and the page number in an in‑text citation;  
* whether the title of a book is italicised or put in quotation marks;  
* how to write the name of a journal, the volume number, and the page range in the reference list;  
* the punctuation marks and spacing that must be used.  

Why do we need a style? Imagine you are reading a recipe book. If every recipe used a different way to list the ingredients—some writing “2 cups flour”, others writing “flour: 2 cups”, and still others writing “flour – 2 cups”—you would spend a lot of time figuring out what each line means. A consistent format saves time for the reader and makes it easy to locate the original source.  

> **In daily life:** Think of a referencing style like the uniform a sports team wears. All players wear the same colours and numbers, so spectators can instantly recognise who belongs to the team. In the same way, a uniform citation format lets readers recognise that a piece of information comes from a particular source.  

The most common styles you will meet in secondary school and the first year of university are:  

1. **APA (American Psychological Association)** – widely used in the social sciences, psychology, education, and some health fields. It places the year of publication right after the author’s name and uses the format (Author, Year).  

2. **MLA (Modern Language Association)** – favoured in literature, language arts, and some humanities subjects. It emphasises the page number and uses the format (Author Page).  

3. **Harvard** – a generic name for author‑date styles that many schools adopt for a variety of subjects. Its basic pattern is similar to APA but with small differences in punctuation and ordering.  

Each style has its own “look” for the reference list (sometimes called a bibliography). For example, APA writes the title of a book in *sentence case* (only the first word and proper nouns capitalised) and italicises the whole title, while MLA capitalises most major words and also italicises the title. Harvard often uses *title case* (capitalising major words) and may or may not italicise, depending on the institution’s specific guide.  

> **Note:** Even within a single style there can be variations. Your school or department may provide a detailed handbook that tweaks the general rules to fit local preferences. Always check the specific guide that your teacher or lecturer has given you.  

When you choose a style, you must apply it consistently throughout the whole document. Switching from APA in one paragraph to MLA in the next is a **common mistake** that makes the work look careless and can confuse the reader.  

> **Common mistake:** Mixing elements from different styles (e.g., using APA’s author‑date format but Harvard’s punctuation) creates an inconsistent reference list that is hard to read.  

Remember that the purpose of a referencing style is not to make writing harder, but to give credit to the original authors and to let anyone who reads your work find the sources easily. By following one set of rules, you show respect for other scholars, avoid plagiarism, and make your own writing look professional.  

> **Remember:** Choose one style, learn its basic rules, and apply them everywhere in your assignment. Consistency is the key to clear, trustworthy academic writing.

sections.heading: Key Elements of In‑Text Citations
sections.body:
When you write an essay or a report, you are building on ideas that other people have already created.  
An **in‑text citation** is the short note you place inside your own sentence that tells the reader exactly where that idea came from.  
It works like a tiny road sign: it points the reader to the full details that you will list later in the reference list.

> **Definition:** An in‑text citation is a brief reference inside the body of your work that includes the author’s name, the year of publication, and, when you quote directly, the page number.

---

### 1. Author name

The author is the person (or people) who wrote the source.  
If the author’s name is part of the sentence, you only need to add the year in parentheses.

*Example:*  
*According to **Smith** (2020), climate change is accelerating faster than expected.*

If the author’s name is not part of the sentence, you put both the name and the year together in parentheses.

*Example:*  
*Recent research shows that sea‑level rise is linked to melting glaciers (Smith, 2020).*

---

### 2. Year of publication

The year tells the reader when the source was made public.  
Including the year helps the reader see how recent the information is and distinguishes between different works by the same author.

*Example:*  
*The theory of cognitive load was first described in the 1990s (Sweller, 1998).*

If you cite two works by the same author from different years, list them both, separated by a comma.

*Example:*  
*Sweller’s early model (1998) differs from his later revision (2010).*

---

### 3. Page number (only when you quote)

A page number is needed when you copy the exact words from a source.  
It lets the reader locate the exact spot in the original text.  
For paraphrases or summaries, a page number is optional (but sometimes required by a specific style).

*Direct quote example:*  
*“Students learn best when information is broken into manageable chunks” (Miller, 2015, p. 42).*

If the quote spans more than one page, use “pp.” and list the range.

*Example:*  
*“The data suggest a clear trend across the decade” (Miller, 2015, pp. 42‑44).*

---

### 4. Putting it all together

You can think of an in‑text citation as a small equation that combines three pieces of information:

$$
\text{Citation} = \text{(Author, Year, Page)}
$$

When you write a **paraphrase** (restating the idea in your own words), you still give credit, but you do not need a page number unless your teacher asks for it.

*Paraphrase example:*  
*Sweller argued that learners have a limited capacity for processing new information (1998).*

When you write a **summary** (condensing the main points of an entire article or chapter), you treat it like a paraphrase: author and year are enough.

*Summary example:*  
*Overall, the study concluded that active learning improves retention more than passive listening (Brown, 2022).*

> **In daily life:** Think of an in‑text citation like a label on a photo you share on social media. You write “Photo by Alex, 2023” so friends know who took it and when, even if they can’t see the full album.

---

### 5. Small tips to avoid common slips

- **Don’t forget the comma** between author and year when both are inside the same parentheses.  
- **Don’t use “&”** inside the narrative part of the sentence; write “and” instead (e.g., *Smith and Jones (2019) found…*).  
- **If there are three or more authors**, write the first author’s name followed by “et al.” (Latin for “and others”).  
  *Example:* *(Taylor et al., 2021).*

> **Common mistake:** Writing *“(Smith 2020)”* without the comma. The correct form is *(Smith, 2020)*.

---

### 6. Quick checklist before you finish a paragraph

1. Did you mention the author’s name?  
2. Did you include the year of publication?  
3. If you quoted directly, did you add the page number?  
4. Are the commas in the right places?

Following these steps ensures that every idea you borrow is clearly marked, which makes your writing trustworthy and helps you avoid plagiarism.

sections.heading: Building a Reference List
sections.body:
When you finish a paper you need one more section: the **reference list** (sometimes called a bibliography). This is a list of every source you mentioned inside the text, written in a fixed order and format so that anyone reading your work can find the original material. Think of it like the “ingredients list” on a food package – it tells you exactly what went into the dish and how much of each ingredient, so you can recreate it if you want.

First, the whole list is placed on a new page after the main body of your essay. The entries are ordered **alphabetically** by the surname (last name) of the first author. If two sources have the same author, you then order them by the year of publication, earliest first. This makes it easy for a reader to scan the list quickly.

### General layout of an entry
Each entry is a single paragraph, but you use a **hanging indent**: the first line starts at the left margin, and all following lines are indented (usually 0.5 inches). This visual cue separates one source from the next.

The basic parts of an entry are:

1. **Author(s)** – surname, followed by initials.  
2. **Year of publication** – in parentheses.  
3. **Title** – only the first word and proper nouns are capitalised (APA/Harvard) or the major words are capitalised (MLA).  
4. **Source details** – this varies with the type of material (book, journal article, website, etc.).  

> **Definition:** *Hanging indent* – a paragraph style where the first line is flush left and all subsequent lines are indented.

### Books
For a printed book the order is:

```
Author, A. A. (Year). Title of the book. Publisher.
```

- **Author**: surname, then a comma, then initials with periods.  
- **Year**: put the year in parentheses, followed by a period.  
- **Title**: italicise the whole title; only the first word and any proper nouns are capitalised (APA/Harvard) or use title case for MLA.  
- **Publisher**: give the name of the company that printed the book; you do not need to add “Co.” or “Ltd.”

*Example*  
Smith, J. L. (2020). *Understanding climate change*. Green Earth Press.

If a book has **two authors**, list them with an ampersand (&) in APA/Harvard or the word “and” in MLA:

```
Brown, P., & Davis, R. (2018). *History of medicine*. Health Press.
```

### Journal articles
A journal article needs the journal name, volume, issue, and page range:

```
Author, A. A. (Year). Title of article. Title of Journal, volume number(issue number), pages.
```

- **Title of article**: sentence case, not italicised.  
- **Title of Journal**: italicised and in title case.  
- **Volume number**: italicised; issue number in parentheses (not italicised).  
- **Pages**: use an en‑dash (–) between the first and last page.

*Example*  
Lee, M. K. (2019). Renewable energy policies in Europe. *Energy Policy*, 45(3), 210–218.

> **Note:** Always include the page range; leaving it out makes it hard for readers to locate the exact article.

### Websites
Web sources add a **URL** (web address) and often a **retrieval date** if the content might change:

```
Author, A. A. (Year, Month Day). Title of page. Site Name. URL
```

If there is no individual author, start with the organization or the title of the page. The date is the day you accessed the page, written as Year, Month Day.

*Example*  
World Health Organization. (2021, March 15). COVID‑19 vaccine safety. WHO. https://www.who.int/vaccine_safety

> **In daily life:** A website citation is like giving a friend the exact link to a YouTube video you mentioned, so they can watch the same clip you saw.

### Other common sources
- **Edited book chapter**: Author of chapter, (Year). Chapter title. In Editor(s) (Eds.), *Book title* (pp. xx‑xx). Publisher.  
- **Conference paper**: Author, (Year). Paper title. In *Proceedings of the Conference Name* (pp. xx‑xx). Publisher.  
- **Report**: Author or organization. (Year). *Title of report* (Report No. xxx). Publisher. URL if online.

### Putting it all together
When you compile the list, check each entry for:

- Correct order of elements.  
- Proper punctuation (commas, periods, parentheses).  
- Italics where required (book and journal titles).  
- Consistent use of the chosen referencing style throughout.

> **Remember:** Consistency is the most important rule. Mixing APA commas with MLA italics will confuse readers and may lose you marks.

Finally, proofread the reference list just as carefully as the main text. A tidy, accurate list shows that you respect the original authors and that you are reliable as a researcher.

sections.heading: Comparing APA, MLA and Harvard
sections.body:
When you look at a bibliography, the three most common styles – APA, MLA and Harvard – all try to give the same information: who wrote the work, when it was published, what the title is, and where it can be found.  
The differences are only in **how** that information is ordered, punctuated and formatted. Knowing the pattern for each style lets you switch between them without having to guess each time.

### 1.  The basic pattern

| Style | Author part | Date part | Title part | Publication part |
|------|-------------|-----------|------------|-------------------|
| **APA** | Last name, Initials. | (Year). | *Title in sentence case.* | Publisher, DOI/URL |
| **MLA** | Last name, First name. | *No parentheses* | *Title in title case* (italic). | Publisher, Year. |
| **Harvard** | Last name, Initials. | (Year). | *Title in sentence case.* | Publisher, DOI/URL |

> **Definition:** *Sentence case* means only the first word and proper nouns are capitalised (e.g., *The impact of climate change*).  
> **Definition:** *Title case* means most major words are capitalised (e.g., *The Impact of Climate Change*).

### 2.  In‑text citations

All three styles place a brief reference inside the text, but they use different punctuation.

- **APA**: (Author, Year) – a comma separates the name and the year, and the whole thing is inside parentheses.  
  Example: *(Smith, 2020)*

- **MLA**: (Author page) – no comma, only the page number follows the name.  
  Example: *(Smith 45)*

- **Harvard**: (Author, Year) – looks like APA, but many institutions add a page number after a comma if needed.  
  Example: *(Smith, 2020, p.45)*

You can think of the in‑text citation as a **mini‑address** that points the reader to the full entry in the reference list, just like a street address points you to a house.

### 3.  Reference‑list formatting

#### a) Order of elements
- **APA**: Author. (Year). *Title*. Publisher. DOI/URL  
  $$\text{APA entry} = \text{Author} + ( \text{Year}) + \text{Title} + \text{Publisher} + \text{DOI}$$
- **MLA**: Author. *Title*. Publisher, Year.  
- **Harvard**: Author, (Year). *Title*. Publisher. DOI/URL  

#### b) Punctuation
- **APA** uses commas after the author and after the year, a period after the title, and a period before the DOI/URL.  
- **MLA** uses periods after the author and after the title, and a comma before the year.  
- **Harvard** mirrors APA’s commas but places a period after the year inside the parentheses.

#### c) Italics and quotation marks
- All three italicise the title of a *book* or *journal*.  
- For *article* titles, APA and Harvard keep them in sentence case without italics, while MLA puts the article title in quotation marks and the journal title in italics.

### 4.  Everyday comparison

Imagine you are writing a shopping list.  

- **APA** is like writing: *Apples, 2 kg, red, bought on 12‑Mar‑2023.* (Name, amount, colour, date) – everything is separated by commas, and the date is in parentheses.  
- **MLA** is like: *Apples 2 kg red, 12‑Mar‑2023.* (Name amount colour, date) – no commas inside the first part, only a final comma before the date.  
- **Harvard** is like: *Apples, 2 kg, red (12‑Mar‑2023).* – similar to APA but the date is inside parentheses after the whole description.

> **In daily life:** Think of the three styles as three different ways to label a photo on your phone: one puts the date first, another puts the location first, and the third mixes both. The picture is the same; only the label changes.

### 5.  Quick checklist for each style

| Step | APA | MLA | Harvard |
|------|-----|-----|---------|
| Author name | Last, Initials. | Last, First. | Last, Initials. |
| Year | (Year). | Year, after publisher. | (Year). |
| Title | *Sentence case* (italic). | *Title case* (italic). | *Sentence case* (italic). |
| Publisher | Publisher, | Publisher, | Publisher, |
| DOI/URL | DOI/URL at end. | Usually omitted in print citations. | DOI/URL at end. |
| In‑text | (Smith, 2020) | (Smith 45) | (Smith, 2020) or (Smith, 2020, p.45) |

> **Remember:** The most reliable way to avoid errors is to copy the exact pattern from a trusted guide (the official APA Manual, MLA Handbook, or your university’s Harvard guide) and then replace the placeholders with your own information.

### 6.  Why the differences matter

Using the correct punctuation and order shows that you respect the conventions of your discipline. It also makes it easy for readers to locate the source quickly. If you mix styles – for example, using an APA author‑date citation with an MLA reference list – the reader will be confused and may doubt the credibility of your work.

By keeping the three patterns in mind, you can choose the style required by your teacher or journal and apply it consistently throughout your paper.

sections.heading: Practice: Choosing and Applying a Style
sections.body:
Imagine you have a short paragraph you want to add to a school essay.  
First you decide **which referencing style** you will use – for example APA, MLA or Harvard.  
Choosing a style is like picking a uniform for a sports team: everyone on the team must wear the same colour so the audience can recognise the group instantly. In academic writing the “uniform” is the set of rules that tells the reader how to find the sources you have used.

### 1. Read the assignment brief  
Often a teacher will tell you which style to use. If the brief is silent, pick one that your school usually teaches (many secondary schools favour Harvard, while many university humanities courses use MLA, and many social‑science courses use APA). Write the name of the style at the top of your worksheet – this reminds you to stay consistent.

### 2. Write a simple paragraph (about 5‑7 sentences)  
Choose a topic you already know, for example “The benefits of daily reading”.  
Do **not** add any citations yet; just write the ideas in your own words.

> **Note:** Keep the paragraph short so you can focus on the citation work, not on polishing the content.

### 3. Identify the three sources you will cite  

| # | Type of source | Example you could use |
|---|----------------|-----------------------|
| 1 | Book | *Reading for Pleasure* by Jane Smith, 2018 |
| 2 | Journal article | “Reading habits of teenagers” by L. Chen, *Journal of Education*, 2020 |
| 3 | Website | “Why reading matters” – article on the National Literacy Council website, accessed 10 Oct 2024 |

Write down the full bibliographic details for each source (author, year, title, publisher, URL, etc.). You will need these later for the reference list.

### 4. Add **in‑text citations** to your paragraph  

Now go back to the paragraph and after each sentence that uses information from a source, insert a citation according to the chosen style.

* **APA** – (Author, Year)  
* **MLA** – (Author Page) – if no page, just the author.  
* **Harvard** – (Author, Year)

For example, in APA:  

> Reading daily improves vocabulary and comprehension (Smith, 2018).  

In MLA:  

> Reading daily improves vocabulary and comprehension (Smith).  

In Harvard:  

> Reading daily improves vocabulary and comprehension (Smith, 2018).

Do this for each of the three sources, making sure the same style is used throughout.

> **In daily life:** Think of in‑text citations like traffic signs. Every time you mention a fact, you put up a sign that points the reader to the “road” (the reference list) where the full directions are given.

### 5. Build the **reference list**  

Create a new page titled “References” (APA), “Works Cited” (MLA) or “Reference List” (Harvard). List the three sources in alphabetical order by the author’s last name. Follow the exact punctuation, italics and order required by the style.

*APA example*  

```
Chen, L. (2020). Reading habits of teenagers. Journal of Education, 45(2), 123‑138.
National Literacy Council. (2024, October 10). Why reading matters. https://www.nlc.org/reading-matters
Smith, J. (2018). Reading for pleasure. Oxford University Press.
```

*MLA example*  

```
Chen, Li. “Reading Habits of Teenagers.” Journal of Education, vol. 45, no. 2, 2020, pp. 123‑138.
National Literacy Council. “Why Reading Matters.” 10 Oct. 2024, www.nlc.org/reading-matters. Accessed 10 Oct. 2024.
Smith, Jane. Reading for Pleasure. Oxford University Press, 2018.
```

*Harvard example*  

```
Chen, L., 2020. Reading habits of teenagers. Journal of Education, 45(2), pp.123‑138.
National Literacy Council, 2024. Why reading matters. [online] Available at: <https://www.nlc.org/reading-matters> [Accessed 10 Oct. 2024].
Smith, J., 2018. Reading for Pleasure. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
```

### 6. Check your work  

1. **Consistency** – every citation in the paragraph must match an entry in the reference list, and the formatting must be the same style throughout.  
2. **Completeness** – no missing information (author, year, title, publisher, URL).  
3. **Alphabetical order** – only for the reference list, not for the in‑text citations.

> **Remember:** The purpose of a reference list is to let anyone reading your work locate the original source quickly, just as a map legend helps you find places on a map.

### 7. Quick self‑test  

- If you change the style, do you know which part of the citation changes?  
- Can you rewrite the same paragraph in a different style without looking at a guide?  
- Does each in‑text citation point to exactly one entry in the reference list?

Practising these steps with a short paragraph builds confidence. Once you can do it for three sources, handling longer essays with ten or twenty sources becomes much easier. Keep a notebook of the most common patterns for each style – it will become your personal cheat‑sheet.

practice.q: What is a referencing style and why do we use it in academic writing?
practice.a: A referencing style is a set of rules that tells you how to show where you got information from. It includes how to write in‑text citations and how to list full details in a reference list. We use it so readers can find the original sources, and to give credit to the authors, which avoids plagiarism.

practice.q: In APA style, how would you cite a book by one author (John Smith) published in 2020 within the text?
practice.a: In APA, an in‑text citation for a single author includes the author's last name and the year of publication. It looks like this: (Smith, 2020). If you mention the author's name in the sentence, you only need the year in parentheses: Smith (2020) argues that …

practice.q: List the three main components that must appear in a reference list entry for a journal article in Harvard style.
practice.a:
In Harvard style, a journal article reference must include:
1. Author(s) – last name and initials.
2. Year of publication in parentheses.
3. Title of the article (sentence case, no quotation marks).
4. Title of the journal (italicised, title case).
5. Volume number (italicised) and, if available, issue number in parentheses.
6. Page range of the article.
(Only three “main components” were asked, so you could summarise them as: author, year, and full source details – which are the author, year, and journal information including title, volume, and pages.)

practice.q: Compare how a direct quote of 25 words is formatted in MLA versus APA style.
practice.a:
MLA: A quotation of more than four lines is set as a block quote. It is introduced with a colon, starts on a new line, is indented one inch from the left margin, double‑spaced, and does not use quotation marks. The in‑text citation (author’s last name and page number) follows after the closing punctuation.
APA: A quotation of 40 words or more is a block quote. It is introduced on a new line, indented 0.5 inches from the left margin, double‑spaced, and does not use quotation marks. The citation (author’s last name, year, and page number) is placed in parentheses after the final punctuation of the quote.
Thus, MLA uses “author page” and APA uses “author, year, page”.

practice.q: You have a source that is a chapter written by two authors (Emily Brown and Michael Green) in an edited book titled *Advances in Climate Science* (edited by Sarah Lee), published in 2018 by Oxford University Press. Write the full reference list entry for this chapter in APA 7th edition, MLA 9th edition, and Harvard style.
practice.a:
APA 7th:
Brown, E., & Green, M. (2018). Title of the chapter. In S. Lee (Ed.), *Advances in Climate Science* (pp. 45‑68). Oxford University Press.
MLA 9th:
Brown, Emily, and Michael Green. “Title of the Chapter.” *Advances in Climate Science*, edited by Sarah Lee, Oxford University Press, 2018, pp. 45‑68.
Harvard:
Brown, E. & Green, M., 2018. Title of the chapter. In: S. Lee, ed., *Advances in Climate Science*. Oxford University Press, pp.45‑68.
(Replace “Title of the chapter” with the actual chapter title; the format shown follows each style’s rules for author order, editors, book title italics, and page range.)

practice.q: A student writes the following in‑text citation: (Johnson, 2015, p. 23). The source is a website with no page numbers. Identify the error and rewrite the citation correctly for APA style.
practice.a: The error is that the citation includes a page number (p. 23) even though the source is a website that does not have page numbers. In APA, for a web source you use the author and year, and if you need to point to a specific part you can use a paragraph number or section heading. The corrected citation could be: (Johnson, 2015, para. 4) if the information is in the fourth paragraph, or simply (Johnson, 2015) if no specific location is needed.

data.recap: A referencing style is a set of rules for citing sources inside your text and listing them in a reference list. In‑text citations give brief details (author, year, page) to point readers to full entries. The reference list, ordered alphabetically, provides complete information for each source. Common styles—APA, MLA, Harvard—use the same data but format it differently.

key_terms.meaning: A collection of guidelines that tell you how to cite sources in the text and how to format the reference list.
A brief note within the body of your work that shows the author, year, and page number (if quoting).
A full list of all sources cited, placed at the end of the document and formatted according to a style.
A paragraph format where the first line starts at the margin and all subsequent lines are indented.
American Psychological Association style, often used in social sciences; author‑date format with specific punctuation.
Modern Language Association style, common in humanities; author‑page format with titles in title case and italics.
An author‑date style similar to APA but with slight differences in punctuation and ordering.
Using the same referencing style throughout a paper so readers can easily locate sources.

quiz.q: What does a referencing style tell you to do?
options: How to cite sources and format the reference list
How to choose a research topic
quiz.why: A referencing style provides rules for citations and reference list formatting.

quiz.q: In an in‑text citation, which element is NOT always required?
quiz.why: Page numbers are only needed for direct quotations.

quiz.q: Which of the following is true about the reference list order?
